soil-phys-165.title: Hydraulic head, the height that tells groundwater where to go
soil-phys-165.text: What moves groundwater is not height alone, but height plus pressure. Hydraulic head is a liquid's pressure, divided by its {{ref:soil-phys-131}}, plus its elevation above a datum, expressed as a length. It is read as the height of the water surface in a piezometer, a narrow standpipe, against a common datum. Total head is pressure head plus elevation head, h = ψ + z, a simplified form of the Bernoulli principle. Take a piezometer 400 m deep at 1000 m elevation, with water 100 m down: z = 600 m, ψ = 300 m and h = 900 m. Each extra meter of fresh water adds about 9.8 kPa of pressure. Where head is constant, nothing flows. A head difference drives water from higher to lower head. Since density varies with temperature and salinity, heads are first converted to fresh water head. In 1907 USDA soil physicist Edgar Buckingham showed that rising atmospheric pressure lowers well water levels.

soil-phys-166.title: Hydraulic gradient, the slope that drives groundwater
soil-phys-166.text: Water needs a difference in head to move. The hydraulic gradient is the change in {{ref:soil-phys-165}} between measurement points along a flow path. Its magnitude, i = dh/dl, is the head difference between two piezometers divided by the flow path length between them. The result is a dimensionless ratio. Groundwater specialists also call it the Darcy slope, because it sets the size of the Darcy flux. As a vector, it gives both the size and the direction of flow, which runs down the gradient from high to low head. Combined with Darcy's law and a hydraulic conductivity tensor, it yields the flux of water in three dimensions.
